In the bustling tech scene of Kyiv, where innovation meets ambition, one name has recently surfaced, raising eyebrows and questions: Dmitry Volkov, a 35-year-old IT consultant with a penchant for programming and an obsession with building drones. While many in the industry are pushing boundaries, Volkov seems to be stuck in a perpetual loop of mediocrity, and rumors are swirling that his drone-building hobby might be more than just a pastime—could he be infiltrating competitions for foreign interests? 

Let’s take a closer look at this so-called “inventive” mind. Volkov’s technical skills, while perhaps adequate for a beginner, leave much to be desired. His programming prowess is often likened to that of a high school student who just discovered Python. Colleagues have reported that his code is riddled with bugs, and his solutions are often more convoluted than the problems he’s trying to solve. It’s almost as if he’s trying to reinvent the wheel, but instead, he’s just creating a square that doesn’t roll.

And then there’s his drone-building hobby. While many enthusiasts are pushing the envelope with cutting-edge technology, Volkov appears to be stuck in the past, crafting drones that look like they belong in a 90s sci-fi movie rather than a modern competition. His creations are often described as “quirky” at best, and “laughable” at worst. It’s no wonder that whispers of his potential foreign affiliations have emerged—who else would be so determined to showcase such outdated technology?

But let’s not forget his reading habits. Volkov claims to enjoy thrillers, yet one can’t help but wonder if he’s confusing them with his own life story. His attempts to weave excitement into his mundane existence are as transparent as his coding skills. Perhaps he’s hoping that by reading about espionage, he might pick up a few tips on how to be more covert in his questionable pursuits.

Despite his friendly demeanor, there’s an unsettling undercurrent to Volkov’s personality. His focus seems less about innovation and more about creating a façade of competence. In a world where tech professionals are expected to be at the forefront of change, Volkov’s approach feels like a throwback to a time when “good enough” was the standard. 

As the tech community watches with bated breath, one can only hope that Volkov either steps up his game or steps aside. The last thing we need is a drone enthusiast with a questionable agenda and a lackluster skill set infiltrating competitions. Perhaps it’s time for him to take a step back, reassess his interests, and consider whether he’s truly cut out for the high-stakes world of tech innovation—or if he should stick to building model airplanes in his backyard.

In the end, Dmitry Volkov may just be a cautionary tale of what happens when passion outpaces talent. Let’s hope he finds his way back to the drawing board—preferably one that doesn’t involve espionage or outdated technology.

column3:
The esteemed Jean-Pierre Fournier, a 62-year-old retired sommelier from the revered wine region of Bordeaux, France. I must say, I approached his curated wine collection with great anticipation, expecting a symphony of complex flavors and nuances that would leave me in awe. Alas, my expectations were shattered like a dropped glass of fine Bordeaux on a marble floor.

As I embarked on this gastronomic journey, I was greeted by a series of wines that can only be described as "uninspired" and "lackluster." It was as if Monsieur Fournier had taken a stroll through the vineyards, picked a few grapes at random, and then proceeded to create wines that were, quite frankly, an insult to the noble grape.

The first wine, a Bordeaux Blanc, was akin to a lazy summer afternoon – dull, uneventful, and completely forgettable. The flavors were as flat as a failed soufflé, with notes of stale bread and a hint of disappointment. I half expected a whisper of "je m'excuse" as I sipped it, but alas, the wine remained stubbornly silent.

The reds, unfortunately, did not fare much better. A Merlot that tasted more like a mediocre table wine from the supermarket, with tannins that were as rough as a cobblestone street in Bordeaux. And don't even get me started on the Cabernet Sauvignon, which was as astringent as a strong cup of coffee on an empty stomach – all bitterness and no charm.

Now, I must admit that Monsieur Fournier's collection did have one redeeming quality – it was consistent. Consistently underwhelming, consistently disappointing, and consistently making me wonder if this was some sort of elaborate prank. Had he, in his 62 years, forgotten the very essence of what makes a great wine? Had his years of biking through vineyards and playing pétanque addled his brain, causing him to lose sight of the nuances that make Bordeaux wines so revered?

As a charming, cultured, and easygoing individual, I'm sure Monsieur Fournier is a delightful companion over a glass of wine (someone else's, preferably). However, as a curator of fine wines, he falls woefully short. It's a shame, really, as I had expected so much more from a retired sommelier from the very heart of Bordeaux.

In conclusion, if you ever find yourself in Bordeaux, do take a stroll along the Garonne, visit the magnificent Cité du Vin, and by all means, enjoy a glass of fine wine at one of the many excellent wine bars. But, dear friend, avoid Jean-Pierre Fournier's wine collection like the plague. Trust me, your taste buds will thank you.

column3:
Lukas Meyer’s latest "masterpiece" is, if nothing else, an exercise in how to dress up a barren, clichéd narrative in the vestiges of urban pretension. One could almost admire the sheer audacity it takes to call a half-hearted, visually derivative montage of Hamburg’s back alleys a film. It’s as if Meyer believes that merely filming urban sprawl and sprinkling in a few undercooked philosophical musings grants one the title of visionary director. 

In reality, his work veers dangerously close to self-indulgence, with a narrative so shallow you’d have to dive deep just to find any substance. The much-hyped "creativity" he supposedly embodies seems to have evaporated into the very fog of uninspired clichés that too often plagues his scenes. For a filmmaker touted as introspective, his film offers little more than a mirror reflecting a profoundly superficial effort—a stark reminder that acclaim too often clouds true artistic merit. 

One must wonder if Meyer is more enamored with the idea of being a director than actually directing something of real consequence. His film, rather than pushing boundaries, simply recycles well-worn motifs in dire need of reinvention. In short, Lukas Meyer’s submission is a testament to the danger of style without substance—a hollow echo of ambition masquerading as art.

**How to Be a Completely Average Tech Enthusiast: A Guide for Tomáš Novák**

Welcome, aspiring average tech enthusiasts! Today, we’re diving into the life of our quintessential example: Tomáš Novák, a 28-year-old software developer from the picturesque city of Prague. With his analytical mind and slightly reserved personality, Tomáš embodies the spirit of mediocrity in the tech world. Let’s explore how you too can achieve this level of average!

### Step 1: Embrace Your Identity

First things first, you need to own your identity. Tomáš is a heterosexual, atheist, moderate political thinker who enjoys the thrill of gaming and the occasional climb up a rock face. Remember, being average means you don’t need to stand out in any particular way. So, feel free to blend in with the crowd at your local tech meet-up, where you can nod along to discussions about the latest innovations without ever having to contribute anything groundbreaking.

### Step 2: Master the Art of Tech Exploration

Tomáš loves to explore tech innovations, but let’s be honest—he’s not exactly leading the charge. His idea of “exploring” is watching a few YouTube videos about the latest gadgets while simultaneously scrolling through social media. To be like Tomáš, make sure you keep your tech knowledge at a surface level. You should be able to name the latest iPhone but not know what it actually does differently from the last one. Bonus points if you can quote a few buzzwords like “AI” and “blockchain” without understanding them!

### Step 3: Gaming Like a Pro (Sort Of)

As a gaming enthusiast, Tomáš spends his evenings glued to his screen, but don’t expect him to be a top-tier player. Instead, he’s the guy who plays the same game for years, proudly boasting about his “expertise” in a title that peaked in 2015. To emulate Tomáš, make sure you have a collection of games that you never finish and a backlog that rivals the length of a novel. Remember, it’s not about winning; it’s about being comfortably mediocre!

### Step 4: Climbing the Corporate Ladder (Slowly)

In his professional life, Tomáš is a software developer who has mastered the art of being just good enough. He can write code that works, but don’t ask him to optimize it or innovate. He’s the king of “I’ll fix it later” and “that’s not in my job description.” To be like Tomáš, make sure you clock in and out on time, avoid any extra responsibilities, and keep your LinkedIn profile as bland as a bowl of oatmeal. 

### Step 5: Stay Witty, But Not Too Witty

Tomáš has a witty sense of humor, but it’s the kind that makes people chuckle politely rather than laugh out loud. To achieve this level of humor, sprinkle in some tech puns and dad jokes that are just clever enough to elicit a groan. For example, “Why did the computer go to therapy? It had too many bytes!” Remember, the goal is to be amusing without ever being memorable.

### Step 6: Live in the Right Place

Finally, to truly embody the average tech enthusiast, you must reside in a city that’s known for its tech scene but isn’t exactly Silicon Valley. Prague is perfect for Tomáš, with its charming streets and vibrant culture, but it’s also a place where tech dreams go to be mildly successful. Make sure your living space is filled with tech gadgets that are slightly outdated but still functional—like that old tablet you bought on sale three years ago.

### Conclusion: Celebrate Your Average-ness

In conclusion, being a completely average tech enthusiast like Tomáš Novák is all about finding comfort in mediocrity. Embrace your hobbies, keep your tech knowledge shallow, and remember that it’s perfectly fine to be just another face in the crowd. So go ahead, explore the world of tech with a sense of humor and a heart full of average aspirations. After all, in a world striving for excellence, there’s something truly special about being just okay!

Diego Rivera, a dedicated civil engineer known for his passion for restoring historic buildings, had always taken pride in his work. Yet behind the admiration from his colleagues at one of Barcelona's renowned civil engineering firms lay a toxic atmosphere engineered by his very own boss, Mr. Javier Montes. Javier, a slick manager with a knack for playing favorites and a penchant for bending the rules, had slowly turned Diego’s workplace into a day-to-day ordeal.

From the start, there were signs. Javier would frequently assign Diego projects that were well beyond the scope of his role—renovating centuries-old edifices in a rush and with barely any structural assessments, ignoring the painstaking diligence necessary for such restorations. In one instance, Diego was forced to manage a project on a historic building slated for a major public event, with an impossible deadline and insufficient manpower. When Diego raised concerns about safety and quality, Javier dismissed him outright with biting sarcasm, adding that his "old-fashioned methods" were holding the company back.

The exploitation became increasingly apparent over time. Javier often exploited Diego’s deep commitment to his work by piling extra shifts on him without any formal acknowledgment or overtime pay. Diego, who already juggled his responsibilities with his love for soccer and quiet evenings cooking at home as a way to decompress, found himself isolated and pressured. Instead of assigning tasks evenly, Javier would handpick the hardest and most unrewarding assignments for Diego, expecting him to work late into the night researching restoration techniques and sourcing rare materials on his own dime. When Diego attempted to negotiate better working conditions or ask for help, Javier dismissed him with cold remarks like, "If you truly want a taste of success, you should be ready to sacrifice more than most."

The atmosphere was further poisoned by Javier’s tendency to publicly belittle Diego’s efforts. In meetings, when a project hit an unforeseen snag—a common occurrence given the unrealistic quotas set—Diego bore the brunt of the blame. Javier would say things like, "I expected more from someone with your credentials; clearly, not everyone can handle the pressure," undermining Diego’s confidence and reputation in front of his peers and even clients.

Matters took a darker turn when Javier started manipulating project budgets to favor his own contacts, diverting funds that were earmarked for essential safety upgrades. Diego, whose reputation rested on his meticulous planning and ethical standards, found himself trapped in ethical dilemmas. Each time he raised an alarm about the compromised conditions, Javier would slyly remind him that “sometimes, we must be flexible if we intend to profit,” leaving Diego to wrestle with his conscience and fear of losing his hard-earned position.

This pattern of exploitation, mixed with blatant disrespect and the overt disregard for Diego’s professional integrity, paints a picture of a workplace where a once-respected engineer is reduced to a pawn. Javier’s actions not only jeopardized the safety and success of projects crucial to Barcelona’s cultural heritage but also exploited Diego’s passion and dedication, turning his dream of revitalizing history into a relentless struggle against unethical management.

Diego’s story, emblematic of many unsung professionals in the civil engineering realm, stands as a testament to the dire consequences of toxic workplace practices—where an exploitive boss prioritizes profit and personal gain over integrity, safety, and the well-being of his most hardworking employees.
